classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate an exponential model, determine its half-life by matching powers of 2, and connect a vertical dilation with unchanged proportional decay. The staged parts guide these linked procedures.

content.prompt: The mass $M$ grams of a certain radioactive substance after $t$ years is modelled by the formula $M=3\times2^{-\frac{1}{53}t}$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the time taken for the mass to halve, called the half-life.

answer.worked:
Half the initial mass is $\frac32$ grams.
$$\begin{align*}\frac32&=3\times2^{-t/53}\\2^{-1}&=2^{-t/53}\\-1&=-\frac{t}{53}\\t&=53.\end{align*}$$
The half-life is $53$ years.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Suppose now that the initial mass is doubled.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Explain this in terms of a dilation and hence write down the new equation for $M$.

answer.worked:
Multiply the mass at each time by $2$, a vertical dilation by factor $2$ from the $t$-axis:
$$\begin{align*}M&=2\left(3\times2^{-t/53}\right)\\M&=6\times2^{-t/53}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: Show that the dilation does not change the value of the half-life.

answer.short: At $t=53$ years, $M=3\text{ g}$, half the new initial mass of $6\text{ g}$. The half-life remains $53$ years.
answer.worked:
For the new model,
$$\begin{align*}M(53)&=6\times2^{-53/53}\\M(53)&=6\times\frac12\\M(53)&=3\text{ g}.\end{align*}$$
This is half the new initial mass of $6\text{ g}$, so the half-life is still $53$ years.
